summary_md: Sutton and Barto's second edition is the standard textbook on reinforcement learning (RL): an agent learns a policy by trial and error so as to maximize cumulative reward. It moves from k-armed bandits and the exploration-exploitation trade-off (Ch. 2), through finite MDPs, dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning (Ch. 3-7), to model-based planning (Ch. 8), function approximation and the deadly triad (Ch. 9-11), eligibility traces, policy gradients, psychology and neuroscience, and case studies (Ch. 16). It contains no social-science data. Its evidence is simulation (on the 10-armed testbed, greedy averages about 1 reward per step against a best of about 1.54) plus reported applications: TD-Gammon after about 300,000 self-play games, AlphaGo Zero after 4.9 million self-play games, and Adobe ad policies scored by high-confidence off-policy evaluation on bank-website logs. For Paul's systems the book is mainly vocabulary and foundation, not evidence. It underlies the RL influence-maximization papers in the vault (Chen 2021 and 2023, RELINK) that Paul maps to the seed gate and the allocator. Measured against the code, the joint CU optimizer is a one-shot, model-based plan. It runs greedy against modeled flip probabilities, never explores, and ingests no observed outcomes (observations=[]). It replans only after modeled threshold crossings. In the book's terms it is pure exploitation of a fixed model, with a myopic single-period objective. The book also sharpens a feasibility limit on Paul's expectation that a learned policy will replace greedy. Its successes needed hundreds of thousands to millions of episodes, but a real CU allocation gives roughly one episode per two-year cycle. Any learned policy would therefore be trained inside the same unvalidated simulator. Section 16.7 points to the more transferable idea: evaluate a candidate allocation policy off-policy from logged contacts and funding, with propensities. The prospective contract does not do this.

bearings.paper_claim: Acting greedily on current value estimates without exploration can lock onto suboptimal actions. On the 10-armed testbed (2000 problems, 1000 steps), greedy averages about 1 reward per step against a best possible of about 1.54, and epsilon-greedy does better in the long run. Planning against a model (Ch. 8) is only as good as the model, and learning requires observed experience.
bearings.system_side: The optimizer allocates the whole $2.5M pot in $500 steps by CELF greedy on modeled pflip marginals. It has no exploration term and no outcome feedback: observations is an empty list reserved for real outcomes. It replans only when a modeled money threshold flips a member's stance state. The docstring already declines to call this an observed adaptive policy. In RL terms it is model-based pure exploitation, so its plan inherits every error in flip_model and money_response.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Exploration only pays when allocation repeats and the outcomes are observed and fed back. For CU giving, rounds are two-year cycles with sparse, confounded outcomes (cosponsorship, votes), so a bandit layer would learn very slowly. The transferable point is the label: the optimum is exact only for the model, not for the world.

bearings.paper_claim: A contextual-bandit (greedy) policy that maximizes immediate reward ignores how actions change future states. In Theocharous et al., an MDP life-time-value policy beat greedy on the LTV metric (clicks per visitor) while greedy won on CTR (clicks per visit). The two metrics diverge: CTR 0.35 versus LTV 1.5 in the illustrative figure.
bearings.system_side: The objective is single-period expected weighted flips, summed over topics. Money given this cycle has no modeled effect on next cycle's receptivity, relationship or stance state, beyond the within-run modeled conversion. Multi-cycle value (access built over repeated giving) is outside the objective.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Holds only if repeated CU giving to the same member changes later responsiveness. That is untested here, and per D-025 it must not be phrased as access or closeness. Any multi-cycle objective would be a new model that needs owner authorization and a second-path reproduction (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: Before deploying a new policy, Adobe estimated its value from data logged under other policies, using high-confidence off-policy evaluation with probabilistic improvement guarantees. Logs: about 200,000 interactions over 7 offers, and 4,000,000 over 12 offers. The test set was served by a random policy.
bearings.system_side: The contract scores frozen predictors by cross-sectional Spearman: seed_prob against new cosponsorship (H1), and pressure_mult against tier movement (H2). Bars are PASS at 0.20 or above, DIRECTIONAL at 0.10 to 0.20, and INDICTED at -0.10 or below, with at least 60 days and 150 movers. It checks that a predictor ranks correctly. It cannot estimate what a different allocation policy would have achieved, because funding and contact are not logged with assignment propensities.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Off-policy evaluation needs logged actions with known or estimable propensities and overlap. Real PAC and lobbying assignment is strategic and near-deterministic, so overlap is poor. Without randomization or a credible propensity model, importance-weighted estimates would have very high variance. Any such estimate stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

gaps_exposed: No component learns from observed outcomes. The optimizer, budget frontier and per-topic allocators all exploit fixed modeled response curves, and none has an exploration or feedback loop. The observations field in optimize.py is reserved but always empty.

The seed gate implements Chen 2021's contingency concept as a hand-set SGATE table (moneyball_core.py:626-630). None of the RL machinery that Paul's cited sources build on (Q-learning, policy learning) is present, and nothing estimates SGATE values from data.

There is no logged-policy record (who was contacted or funded, when, and with what propensity), so the off-policy evaluation of alternative allocation policies described in Sec. 16.7 is not possible yet.

The allocation objective is single-cycle. Effects that carry across cycles from repeated giving are not modeled, so a myopic-versus-long-horizon comparison (the CTR-versus-LTV contrast) cannot be run.
flags: Metadata: the item kind is academic-article, but the work is a textbook (2nd edition, 2020 printing). No DOI is needed.

Feasibility caution, not a brain-rule conflict: the book's RL successes used 300,000 to 4.9 million training episodes. Any learned allocation policy for Melange would be trained in the simulator, not on real cycles. Its outputs would inherit simulator error and would stay UNVERIFIED (DE-062) until reproduced by a second path.

Sec. 11.3 deadly triad: combining function approximation, bootstrapping and off-policy training risks divergence. A GCOMB-style learned replacement for greedy trained off-policy on sparse legislative data would combine all three.
paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations or entries on this book. His position on the joint optimizer (adaptive greedy plus CELF now, a learned policy such as GCOMB later at scale) is consistent with the system as built, and that note is not stale: the code is still CELF greedy with no learned policy. The book qualifies the second half of his expectation. Learned policies earn their advantage through very large numbers of episodes, which real CU allocation cannot supply, so a learned policy would only learn the simulator. His Chen 2021 mapping is built as a fixed SGATE table.

related.why: Applies RL from this book to contingency-aware seeding, which is the source Paul maps to SGATE in the seed gate.
RL for influence maximization under complex contagion, which Paul ties to LT priming. It uses the value-function and policy-learning machinery of Ch. 6 and 9-13.
Deep RL for closed-network edge activation. It extends the book's function-approximation methods to influence maximization.
Original Q-learning paper. The book presents Q-learning in Sec. 6.5 with its convergence context.
Potential-based reward shaping, which matters if a simulator-trained allocation policy were given shaped rewards such as partial flips.
Gives guarantees for greedy policies that adapt to observed outcomes without learning a value function. This is the non-RL alternative the optimizer already cites as a diagnostic bound.
Multi-agent RL application built on the single-agent foundations in this book; adjacent, with no direct bearing on Melange.
